title: A look at Dead Belt and the Penguin Library Science Fiction postcards
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=akC-r5hlDkc

Daniel (@dungeondive) takes a look at Dead Belt, a solo RPG about space salvagers he pitches to fans of Void Bastards and Cowboy Bebop, and one whose real subject is debt. Every run costs upkeep, upgrades raise that upkeep, and the bank may compound your interest while you are out, so you can come home from a derelict with less than you left with. Your stats are the resources you spend: gas for oxygen, grit and gear for rerolls, glow for light, load for carrying capacity.

The hook is that ships are built from a deck of ordinary playing cards, laid out in the pattern for whichever tier of wreck you rolled. The red joker is your airlock, the black joker your payday, and each flipped card reveals its module by suit: clubs are barriers, spades are bad news, diamonds are salvage, and red cards can be pushed for more. Marked break lines show where the hull may separate, forcing spacewalks. Every move rolls a d6 against your oxygen, and ones eat a tank at an escalating rate. On camera Daniel turns over his first card and finds the payday, a one-in-fifteen chance he had never hit before. He wishes barriers were more than a prompt and a roll, and wants a paperback-sized printing to keep open on the table.

The second half flips through the Penguin Science Fiction postcards, a hundred classic covers from Roadside Picnic to The Circus of Dr. Lao, one of his favourite books.

----

Dead Belt uses an ordinary deck of cards as the ship you explore. What is the best use of a standard playing-card deck you have seen in a solo game?
